planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in gritty, well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; this older, reliable selection is propagated by cuttings or division to keep its compact habit true.

directions: 'Alexander's White' is a long-grown, densely branching selection of evergreen candytuft forming a tidy mound of narrow, glossy dark-green leaves that stays neat and full-bodied through the growing season. In mid-spring it produces an especially heavy flush of pure white, flattened flower clusters that nearly obscure the foliage, holding bloom slightly longer than seed-grown candytuft. Grow in gritty, well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, where it tolerates poor rocky ground and drought once established but declines in wet or heavy clay. Shear back by about a third right after flowering to keep the mound tight and to prevent the woody base from opening up and splaying over time.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; this reblooming selection benefits from a light shearing after the main spring flush to encourage its second flowering later in the season.

directions: 'Autumn Snow' is a reblooming selection of evergreen candytuft, producing the typical heavy flush of pure white flower clusters over glossy dark-green foliage in mid-spring and then, unlike most candytuft cultivars, sending up a lighter secondary bloom in late summer to early fall. Grow in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; consistent drainage is essential, as it is prone to crown rot in heavy or poorly drained ground. Shear the plant back lightly after the spring bloom fades to tidy the mound and to promote the fall rebloom, and avoid heavy fertilizing, which encourages lax, floppy growth at the expense of flowers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; deadheading and a light post-bloom shearing help this compact selection produce its characteristic light fall rebloom.

directions: 'October Glory' is a compact, dense-mounding candytuft selection valued for combining a heavy mid-spring flush of pure white flowers with a dependable light rebloom in early fall, giving two seasons of interest from a single planting. Grow in gritty, well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, since good drainage is more important to its health than soil fertility. It handles poor, rocky soil and drought well once established, making it dependable for edging, walls, and rock garden pockets. Shear lightly after the spring bloom to keep the mound tight and to encourage the fall flush, and avoid winter wet, which is the most common cause of losses.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; this large-flowered selection is propagated by cuttings or division to keep its distinctive white-eyed color true.

directions: 'J.S. Baker' is a striking aubrieta selection bearing unusually large, deep reddish-purple flowers, each marked with a small but distinct white eye at the center, in a dense spring flush over a low mat of soft, grayish-green leaves. Grow in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; it is well suited to dry stone walls, gravel gardens, and rock garden edges where sharp drainage keeps the crown from rotting. It tolerates poor, rocky soil and drought once established but struggles in hot, humid summers. Shear hard immediately after flowering to keep the mat dense, prevent the center from opening up, and encourage strong bloom the following spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; raised at Bressingham Gardens, this double-flowered pink selection is increased by cuttings or division to keep it true.

directions: 'Bressingham Pink' is a double-flowered aubrieta selection raised at England's Bressingham Gardens, bearing rounded, fully double, clear pink flowers held tightly above a low mat of small, soft green leaves. Grow in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like other aubrieta it is prone to root and crown rot in heavy, wet, or acidic ground. It is a good choice for dry walls, gravel gardens, and rock garden edges, where its cascading habit shows to best effect. Shear back hard right after flowering to keep the mat compact, encourage fresh growth, and promote strong flowering the following spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; this deep-colored, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection is propagated by cuttings or division to keep its rich color true.

directions: 'Gurgedyke' is a vigorous aubrieta selection holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bearing an exceptionally dense spring flush of rich reddish-purple flowers over a low, spreading mat of small, soft gray-green leaves. Grow in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; it is an excellent choice for dry stone walls, gravel gardens, and the edges of raised beds, where its trailing habit can cascade freely. It tolerates poor, rocky soil and short dry spells once established but performs poorly in hot, humid summer conditions. Shear the plant back hard immediately after flowering to keep growth dense and to encourage a strong repeat display the following spring.

common_name: Flore Pleno Alpine Rock Cress (Double White)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into gritty, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this semi-double form sets little to no seed and is increased only by division or cuttings.

directions: 'Flore Pleno' is a semi-double-flowered selection of alpine rock cress, producing dense racemes of pure white flowers with extra petals that give the spring display a fuller, longer-lasting look than the single-flowered species. Grow in gritty, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like the species it rots quickly in wet or waterlogged ground, especially over winter. Because the doubled flowers rarely set viable seed, the plant spreads only by its rosettes and must be propagated by division or cuttings to keep the true form in circulation. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain a tight, mounded mat and encourage fresh rosette growth.

planting.note: Sow direct in early spring or fall, or plant divisions, into gritty, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this pink-flowered form is a popular alternative to the white-flowered species for softer spring color schemes.

directions: 'Rosea' is a pink-flowered selection of alpine rock cress, forming the same low, mat-forming rosettes of grayish-green, softly hairy leaves as the species but covering itself in early spring with dense racemes of soft pink, four-petaled flowers rather than white. Grow in gritty, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential, as the plant rots readily in wet or heavy soil, particularly in winter. It pairs well with the white species form and with purple aubrieta and golden basket-of-gold in the classic spring rock garden palette, softening the display with an added pink tone. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat compact and encourage vigorous fresh growth.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown clumps in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full shade; this old Belgian hybrid between Clivia miniata and Clivia nobilis blooms most reliably after a cool, dry 6-8 week winter rest, like its parent species.

directions: Grow in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to bright shade, keeping roots slightly pot-bound to encourage flowering. Clivia x cyrtanthiflora was raised in Belgium around 1899 by crossing Clivia miniata with the smaller-flowered, pendulous Clivia nobilis, and the resulting hybrid combines traits of both parents: broad, dark, strap-shaped leaves closer to C. miniata in size, topped by nodding umbels of narrower, tubular, orange-red flowers with distinct green tips that hang downward rather than facing outward as in typical C. miniata hybrids. Flowering occurs in late winter to spring on sturdy scapes above the evergreen foliage, followed by decorative berries that color slowly over many months. As with other clivias, avoid overwatering during the winter rest period and disturb the roots as little as possible, since recovery from division is slow.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this English selection, raised at Chettle House in Dorset, stays noticeably more compact and upright than Walker's Low and rarely needs staking.

directions: Chettle Blue forms a neat, sturdy clump of soft grey-green foliage topped with dense spikes of lavender-blue flowers over a long summer season. It holds its shape far better than many faassenii-type catmints, resisting the flopping habit that afflicts taller selections, which makes it a favorite for tidy border edges and pathside plantings. Shear the whole plant back by about half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom into autumn. Once established it shrugs off heat, drought, and poor soil, and its flowers draw bees and other pollinators steadily through the season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; named for Bramdean House in Hampshire, this grandiflora selection is taller and more richly colored than Six Hills Giant and benefits from a bit more moisture.

directions: Bramdean sends up tall, well-branched stems of coarsely toothed, deep green leaves crowned with unusually large, richly violet-blue flowers held in whorled spikes through summer. Its bigger flowers and deeper color set it apart from smaller catmints, and its upright habit suits the middle or back of a mixed perennial border rather than edging duty. Cut stems back hard after the first bloom flush to keep growth dense and to prompt a second wave of flowers into early autumn. It tolerates average garden soil and some afternoon shade better than most catmints, and bees work its flowers heavily all season.
